title: A Portrait for the Confession
premise: When a water-damaged diary washes up behind Oscar Reyes's failing bookshop, the entries continue for months past the date Marina Voss disappeared from the coastal town of Greyhaven—entries written in a hand Oscar recognizes, because he taught it to write cursive. As Oscar and the diary's finder, teenage runaway Wren, retrace Marina's final months, they uncover that her disappearance was staged to escape an abusive husband, and that the town's most respected citizens—including Oscar's old partner—helped her vanish and then buried the truth to protect themselves. The diary's final entries reveal Marina has been alive nearby all along, watching, until her husband's death freed her to come home. Oscar must choose between exposing the conspiracy that cost him his career and honoring the silence that kept a woman alive, ultimately brokering a confession that reopens the case just enough to give Marina her name back—before the tide gives up what it took.
about_author: Ulyana Yarrow spent a decade cataloging rare maritime diaries in a secondhand bookshop on the Oregon coast before turning to fiction. Her mysteries explore what small towns keep in their ledgers, and what it costs to read them.

chapters.title: Watermarks
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A winter storm floods the bookshop's basement, and among the ruined stock Oscar finds a diary with a tide-stained cover. He recognizes the handwriting as Marina Voss's—the missing woman whose case ended his career fifteen years ago. The last entry is dated eight months after she vanished. Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashbacks interleave with the present as Oscar catalogs the town's secrets he's kept filed away: who paid whose debts, who left whose bed. Wren, a teenage runaway sleeping in his storeroom, catches him reading the diary and demands in. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being a keeper of secrets.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reads the diary aloud and notices the entries shift from fear to strange calm after the disappearance date—Marina writes about watching the town from somewhere close. Wren, who ran from her own home, feels an unsettling kinship with a woman who may have done the same. Emotional beat: recognition across time.

chapters.title: The Husband's House
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar visits Dale Voss's widow, Ruth, under the pretense of buying books. Ruth mentions Dale died last spring, and that Marina's mother still leaves flowers at an empty grave. Oscar notices a fresh cursive inscription inside a donated novel—Marina's hand, dated three months ago. Emotional beat: the past pressing through floorboards.

chapters.title: What the Partner Knew
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar confronts his former partner, Ed Calloway, now the town's beloved sheriff emeritus, who warns him off with genuine fear: 'You were the only one who believed she drowned. Be glad you were wrong.' Ed reveals nothing but confirms the case was closed by order, not evidence. Emotional beat: betrayal wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: Runaway Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren calculates the diary's timeline against tide charts and realizes the final entries describe the bookshop itself—Marina has been watching the shop. Wren hides this from Oscar, terrified he'll stop needing her if the mystery solves itself. Emotional beat: the fear of becoming unnecessary.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the decommissioned lighthouse, Oscar finds a ledger of small payments spanning fifteen years—hush money from five town families, signed off by Ed. Someone has been funding a hidden life. The most recent payment is dated last month. Emotional beat: the machinery of mercy and cover-up revealed as the same machine.

chapters.title: Five Families, One Silence
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar works through the five signatories: the bank manager, the doctor, the pastor, the harbormaster, and Ed. Each had a reason—Dale Voss had dirt on all of them, and Marina knew everything. Helping her vanish bought the town's silence. Emotional beat: complicity dressed as kindness.

chapters.title: Wren's Own Missing Date
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Oscar discovers Wren's real name and that she's a missing person too, her face on flyers he's been using as bookmarks. The confrontation is quiet and devastating: two people who survived by disappearing, one asking the other why she stayed gone. Emotional beat: being seen against your will.

chapters.title: The Tide Chart Alibi
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Reconstructing the night Marina vanished, Oscar realizes the 'drowning' was staged during a storm surge that destroyed all physical evidence—the tide was the accomplice. But one thing couldn't be faked: the diary's later entries prove she lived, meaning someone committed no murder but everyone committed obstruction. Emotional beat: the case reframing itself in his hands.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading Back
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The diary gains a new entry while in their possession—addressed to Oscar by name. Marina is watching them, frightened that exposure will end the fragile life she's built. Wren writes back, hiding the exchange from Oscar, negotiating with a ghost. Emotional beat: correspondence with the presumed dead.

chapters.title: Ed's Confession, Partial
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Ed admits he helped stage the disappearance after Marina came to him with a broken wrist and proof of Dale's crimes against the five families. 'The town needed a drowning more than it needed a scandal.' He refuses to say where she went, and threatens to expose Oscar's own falsified report from fifteen years ago. Emotional beat: two compromised men circling the truth.

chapters.title: The Falsified Report
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashback to the original investigation: Oscar's report declared the drowning accidental because Ed showed him evidence that Marina's mother would be destroyed by the truth. Oscar signed it to protect the mother, and it cost him his badge anyway when the family cried cover-up. Emotional beat: understanding that he's been paying for a mercy all along.

chapters.title: Ruth Voss Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren befriends Ruth Voss, who confesses she's known Marina was alive for years—Dale's death freed her, but Marina won't come home because coming home means the lie collapses and the five families fall with it. Ruth begs Wren to let sleeping wives lie. Emotional beat: grief for a marriage that was itself a disappearance.

chapters.title: The Harbormaster's Boat
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The harbormaster, cornered, admits he ferried Marina to a cabin up the coast the night she vanished and has kept the payments flowing since. He gives Oscar coordinates but warns that Ed will bury Oscar the way the tide buried the evidence. Emotional beat: crossing the point of no return.

chapters.title: Cabin at Mile Nine
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar finds the cabin empty but lived-in, the diary's companion journals on the shelf—fifteen years of a hidden life, including pages about him: 'the detective who almost believed me.' Marina has been forty miles away the whole time. Emotional beat: the ache of being watched by someone you failed.

chapters.title: Wren Runs Again
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Terrified that the truth will send her back to her own family, Wren steals the diaries and buys a bus ticket. At the station she reads Marina's final journal—about how hiding stopped being survival and started being a smaller kind of drowning—and turns back. Emotional beat: choosing to belong over choosing to vanish.

chapters.title: The Meeting at the Tide Line
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Using Wren's returned diaries and a note left in the shop, Oscar arranges a dawn meeting on the beach. Marina appears—older, watchful, unrepentant. She offers him the truth on one condition: the five families stay standing, because their guilt is the only wall between her and a town that would devour her story. Emotional beat: two survivors negotiating terms.

chapters.title: What Ed Would Burn
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Ed, learning of the meeting, moves to destroy the lighthouse ledger and pin the obstruction on Oscar. Oscar anticipates him, having already given copies to Ruth and the pastor—turning the conspiracy's own keepers into its witnesses. The confrontation in the bookshop ends with Ed's choice: go down alone or help write an honest ending. Emotional beat: the climax of loyalty versus truth.

chapters.title: A Portrait for the Confession
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The resolution: a closed-door statement, carefully worded—Marina Voss, victim of sustained abuse, fled with assistance; her death record is corrected; the five families accept quiet sanctions; Ed retires under review rather than prosecution. Marina gives a statement but not a face, a portrait in words only. Oscar signs his own amended report at last. Emotional beat: truth delivered at the highest price it could bear.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Buys Paperbacks
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, a woman with grey in her hair browses the shop and buys a paperback of sea poems, paying with exact change and a nod Oscar doesn't acknowledge. Wren watches her leave and understands: some returns are meant to be invisible. Emotional beat: quiet joy, the mystery resolved but never fully told.

chapters.title: Shelf by Shelf
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Spring: Wren stays, enrolled in school under Oscar's guardianship; the bookshop takes a new sign; the diary goes into a locked drawer, not the evidence file. Oscar alphabetizes nothing that night, instead writing his own first entry in a fresh notebook. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, survival paid for, and the tide keeping what it keeps.
